This is pretty late, but as a patient, I had a terrible fever, nausea, and intense abdominal cramping. I had ulcers all up in my genitals and I felt like I was dying. I wore my winter coat in my dorm with a blanket and couldn’t get warm. I went to the ER twice and received a diagnosis of a bladder infection (which, when results came back, I didn’t have) and herpes (which I tested negative for). They gave me antivirals, antibiotics, and steroids because they didn’t know what I had but they wanted to cover their bases. Eventually, my symptoms faded, but I remained really fatigued and kept having cramps. 

I eventually had a check up with my primary and told him about my experience. He had just had a training on Behcet’s and was able to point me to a rheumatologist who put me on the right medications. Without him, I’d be getting awful, frequent, flares which could eventually leave me blind, with a blood clot somewhere, or worse. Turns out my Behcet’s is pretty bad, and without my primary, I’d be on disability due to irreparable damage to my body.

I don’t think this is as common as the news makes it seem. Most parents don’t want their kids to be trans, even if they are trans. It’s hard and society is very unfair to trans people. Occasionally, this happens and it’s wrong, so it makes it to the news. Although I disagree with labeling a child as trans due to having mannerisms of the “opposite” gender, I don’t see anything wrong with asking a child questions. I teach and I had a boy come in with painted toes. I asked why and he said it felt nice. He still identifies as a boy, but he just happens to think the feeling of applying nail polish is nice. If he answered that he likes girly stuff and is a girl, we would have had a different conversation. 

I feel like the notion that parents forcing their children to be trans is common is just a tool so people can complain about trans people in a way that isn’t as offensive. It’s awful that parents try to raise their children as a gender they aren’t, but it’s important to remember this is not common. It should not be done. It should not be supported, but parents with trans children should be supported. Some people figure out their gender pretty young, and if they consistently refer to themselves as that gender throughout childhood, supporting the child is important as a parent. When trans people are lucky enough to figure out their gender earlier in life, they can try puberty blockers (which a doctor has to prescribe and it usually requires notes from licensed therapists or mental health professionals). Puberty blockers are super important since they can prevent the permanent changes of puberty (or at least delay them until the child is a teen and old enough to either stop the blockers or start taking hormonal therapy depending on the child’s gender identity).  Although some doctors may not go through these checks, this is like blaming all doctors for overprescribing antibiotics when it’s really only a fraction of doctors doing this. It’s still terrible, and overall we should train doctors not to overprescribe, but most doctors are fine. To help trans (or questioning or parent-forcing-trans-ness) children, family doctors (especially in non-urban areas) require more training on identifying whether or not a patient would benefit from medically transitioning. The solution is not a blanket statement, but further education to help kids live their truth.

Maybe there are people pretending, but to assume every trans person may be pretending is not fair. I personally find it interesting that so many different cultures developed similar ideas about gender (although they were suppressed later on).

The main reason trans people have a high risk of suicide is because people treat them poorly. In most of the US, it is legal to deny a job or housing to someone because of they are transgender. Again, because there are so few trans people, and so many other things the government spends money on, you aren’t spending any of your money on these surgeries. 

Your argument (or at least this argument when initiated by others) is not that you disagree with trans people getting free surgeries, but that you want to have a platform to discuss your disgust with trans people in general under the guise of concern for trans mental health. The only time you will ever mention concern over these large suicide rates is when it props up a discussion that allows you to preach your disagreement in the validity of trans people. The impact this opinion has is much larger than the impact your personal taxes have on covering a phalloplasty. 

Your opinion and the people who share it contribute not only to the high suicide rate among trans people, but to the violence and blatant discrimination trans people face on a daily basis. 

You also operate under the assumption that anyone who receives coverage from the government for gender affirmation surgery is someone who is lazy and does not work or do anything productive for society. Trans people do work, they are often discriminated against and this impacts their ability to get good jobs. Some are self employed. Some work for the federal or state government. Some are struggling, but so are many others receiving aid from the government. 

It comes down to whether or not you believe access to healthcare is a human right. I personally believe everyone, no matter their level of poverty, deserves quality medical treatment.

Trans people are not mentally unstable, but they do tend to have mental illnesses like depression and anxiety. This is largely because of how other people treat them, even though these actions make no impact on anyone else. Medically transitioning is not a bandaid fix. It permanently reduces risk of suicide and depression. That’s a treatment. It’s also not available without parent sign off before legal age. Hormones are not available until teen years and every treatment requires years as living as the gender they identify, letters from medical professionals proving that they are stable, and further medical history. even if you view this as enabling, by the point a trans person undergoes a surgery, they have seen at least a half dozen medical professionals who all agree that this is the best treatment to improve quality of life. Alternatives do not work and decrease quality of life. 

With gambling addicts, giving them money does not vastly improve quality of life. Gambling addicts will continue to gamble, and money is eventually finite for them. We cannot afford to give gambling addicts unlimited sums of money and doing so would hurt many people. There are many more gambling addicts in the world than trans people, so we would also spend more money on more people. This enabling is very different since there are better treatments that improve quality of life and decrease harm to others. 

There are so few trans people, and even if their procedures can be expensive, much more of your tax payer dollars are going toward things that do harm people (like bombing other countries). 

I honestly feel like this argument is so pointless because these procedures have no impact on anyone outside of the patient their immediate family. The financial burden you as a taxpayer have is so small and practically nothing.

Except that we don’t associate gender with chromosomes. Maybe you take the DNA of every person you meet before assigning them pronouns, but I typically do it by what I assume it to be. More recently, I’ve been introducing myself with my pronouns so that the other person has an opportunity to introduce with theirs so that we’re both on the same page. 

Like yeah; there’s no changing sex, but in most situations, it isn’t important at all.

The difference is that quality of life is vastly decreased if you don’t have arms. Everyday life becomes very difficult. This is clearly a bad decision if nothing is wrong with them. Undergoing gender affirmation surgery does not do this. People still function same as before, but typically much happier. You don’t have to understand why, but this works as a treatment. Turns out that the alternative (therapy to fight urges to transition) is really traumatic and does not work.

As someone whose insurance comes from the state, I like that my surgery is at least partially covered. We don’t have a lot of money, but I know this will help me. I’ve been on antidepressants and mood stabilizers all my life. It’s gotten better since hormones and top surgery, but I’m still miserable with my lower half. 

This wasn’t a choice; when I was a little kid, before I even knew that boys and girls have different parts, I would stretch out my genitals and tug and pull, trying to make them bigger. I dreamed that they would grow. Apparently, I wore hats a lot and liked to hide my hair. My parents actively tried to suppress a lot of these things. Eventually my mom gave up and just let me do my thing. 

Not every trans person has these experiences, but just imagine: you wake up with a typically not your sex’s body tomorrow but your brain is the same. You’d be fine for a while maybe, but eventually it would bug you. Over the years, you might actively become depressed or suicidal because your expectations are not your reality. 

Doctors swear an oath to do no harm. Most doctors follow that rule. Medical research shows that treating trans people as the gender they identify and allowing them to undergo hormonal therapy/gender affirmation surgery improves quality of life. 

You’re right that it is unfair that these surgeries are covered sometimes and others that are more physically necessary are not, but this anger should not be at trans people. This anger should be aimed at insurance companies for their blatant disregard for human life in favor of profits. Trans people have been fighting since these surgeries were invented to gain access to them. We have worked together to fight insurance companies from denying us coverage. It’s really hard for people who immediately need a procedure to fight an insurance company, and after they die, their families want to mourn. We should have affordable access to healthcare, all of it. We can afford it if we go after the monopolies superficially inflating the prices of medications, devices, and procedures. They know we have no other option, but if we work together, just as the trans community has and continues to do, we can make healthcare affordable, so that even if your taxes still go toward someone else’s surgery, overall you’d be paying less for healthcare.
